planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Texas palafox grows naturally on deep sand deposits and sandy roadsides across central and south Texas and self-seeds readily in similar loose, dry soil.

directions: Direct sow into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Texas palafox is a tall, wiry native annual of deep-sand habitats across central and south Texas, producing loose, airy clusters of fragrant, pale to deep pink flowers with long, prominent, needle-like stamens from summer through fall that give the plant its common name and draw a steady stream of bees and butterflies. It is highly adapted to loose, infertile sand and gravel where richer garden soil actually works against it, so avoid heavy amendment or fertilizer and let it grow lean and tall as it does in the wild. Once introduced to a suitably sandy, sunny site it self-seeds readily, returning reliably each year, and its airy, see-through form works well massed at the back of a native wildflower meadow or scattered through a xeric gravel garden.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into dry, lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; lacy tansyaster is a tough Great Plains and Southwest native that flowers best with minimal water and no supplemental fertility.

directions: Direct sow into dry, lean, well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; lacy tansyaster is a short-lived native perennial of dry prairies, rocky slopes, and roadsides from the Great Plains west into the desert Southwest, producing finely divided, spiny-toothed foliage and abundant bright yellow, daisy-like flowers over a long summer-into-fall bloom season. It is exceptionally drought- and heat-tolerant once established, thriving in the same lean, sun-baked, rocky conditions that stress most garden perennials, and rich, moist soil or regular fertilizer tends to shorten its life and reduce flowering. A dependable, low-maintenance filler for a xeriscape, gravel garden, or dry native wildflower border, it self-seeds modestly in favorable open, sunny sites to maintain a sustained population.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas dandelion is a common winter-annual roadside wildflower across the southern Great Plains and Gulf South, self-seeding readily once introduced.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas dandelion produces a low rosette of narrow, deeply lobed leaves and, despite the misleading common name, pale lavender-pink rather than yellow, dandelion-like flowers on slender stalks in spring, followed by fluffy seed heads relished by goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. It is a common, easygoing winter annual of roadsides, pastures, and open fields across the southern Great Plains and Gulf South, thriving in ordinary, unimproved soil with little care beyond a sunny to lightly shaded spot. Once introduced it self-seeds readily, naturalizing in a native wildflower meadow or informal lawn alternative, and its early, extended spring bloom period provides useful nectar for small native bees ahead of the main spring wildflower flush.
